title: Upakosala and the fires (4.10–4.15)
hook: a student tends his teacher's fires for twelve years and is never sent home; then the fires themselves begin to teach

segments.voice: Yesterday: the bull, the fire, the swan and the diving bird, Satyakama's four unlikely teachers. Your line was the whole world teaches. What taught you something yesterday? Week two of year two begins. Day three hundred thirty-seven.

Satyakama grows up and becomes a teacher himself. And now he has a student of his own, Upakosala. For twelve years, Upakosala lives in his teacher's house and tends the sacred fires, keeping them fed, morning and evening. Other students come and finish and are sent home. Not him. Then Satyakama leaves on a journey, still without teaching him. And Upakosala, the text says, is so sad he stops eating. The teacher's wife begs him: eat something. He says no. I'm full of sorrow. And that's when the fires he's been tending for twelve years start to talk.
screen: `TWELVE YEARS TENDING THE FIRES.` → `EVERYONE ELSE GOES HOME.` → `HE STOPS EATING.`

segments.voice: The fires confer among themselves. This student has served us well. Let's teach him. And together they tell him: breath is Brahman. Ka is Brahman. Kha is Brahman. Upakosala is honest: I understand breath is Brahman, but I don't understand ka and kha. Ka means joy. Kha means space. And the fires explain that they're one: the joy that is also space, the space that is also joy. Then each of the three fires teaches him about itself, and about the sun, the moon, the lightning, the waters. Then they say: we've told you our part. Your teacher will tell you the way. When Satyakama comes home, he looks at his student and says what was said to him years ago: your face shines like someone who knows Brahman. Who taught you? Upakosala, a little embarrassed, glances at the fires. Satyakama listens, and then says: they told you about the worlds. I'll tell you the rest. As water doesn't cling to a lotus leaf, wrongdoing doesn't cling to one who knows this. And the teaching he gives is this: the person you see in the eye, that is the self, that is Brahman, deathless and fearless. Notice the shape of it. The fires teach the outer things. The teacher points inward, to the one looking out through the eyes. The story keeps both: Upakosala needed his teacher, and he needed the fires. But where everything finally points is the seer inside.
screen: `THE FIRES DECIDE TO TEACH.` · `KA IS JOY. KHA IS SPACE.` · `WATER ON A LOTUS LEAF.` · `THE PERSON SEEN IN THE EYE.` · then, large: `THE TEACHER WITHIN.`

segments.voice: Today's practice turns from the fire to the one watching it. Sit and settle. If you have a candle, you can light it and look at it; if not, look at any small light. Watch it for a few breaths: the flicker, the color. Then gently notice that there is someone seeing it. Don't try to find that someone. Just rest in the fact of seeing. Joy and space, ka and kha. The bell holds the time.
Upakosala and the fires. A student who tended the sacred fires for twelve years; the fires taught him about the world, and his teacher pointed him to the self within.
Your line: the teacher within. Today, before you look something up or ask someone, pause for one breath and ask yourself first what you already know. Day three hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: In the traditional guru-shishya relationship, a Hindu student serves and lives with a teacher for years; many Hindus also speak of an inner guide, and of the outer teacher as one who points the student inward.

fork.reveal: he won't eat. and in his grief the fires he has tended for twelve years decide to teach him.

original.note: Sanskrit ācārya: teacher, the one who teaches by conduct. the fires tell Upakosala that his ācārya will show him the way.

trapdoor: what you thought: magic fires that talk.
what it means: the outer world teaches about the worlds; the teacher points to the seer inside the eye.
what a scholar hears: Chandogya 4.10–4.15. ka (joy) and kha (space) as one Brahman, and the lotus-leaf simile of 4.14.3.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 4.10 (Upakosala's twelve years; the fires teach: breath, ka, kha)
Chandogya Upanishad 4.14–4.15 (the lotus leaf; the person seen in the eye)

notes: Upakosala Kamalayana; the script uses Upakosala only.

Each of the three fires (garhapatya, anvaharyapacana/dakshina, ahavaniya) teaches about itself and a set of correlates (earth, food, fire, sun; waters, quarters, stars, moon; breath, space, sky, lightning). The script compresses these to 'the sun, the moon, the lightning, the waters'; confirm.
Lotus-leaf simile (4.14.3) and 'the person seen in the eye is the self, deathless and fearless, Brahman' (4.15.1): paraphrased; confirm.
Carry 'the teacher within' is the outline's; the text keeps both outer teacher and inner seer, which the script says.
